newsitem.title: USA: U.S. worker compensation up 0.8 percent in quarter.
newsitem.headline: U.S. worker compensation up 0.8 percent in quarter.

text.p: American workers' overall compensation gains picked up modestly in the second quarter of 1997 as a rebound in benefit costs helped offset a slight slowing in wage and salary growth, the government said on Tuesday.
Pay and benefits together rose 0.8 percent in the second quarter after a 0.6 percent gain in the first three months, the Labor Department said in its quarterly Employment Cost Index.
The overall 0.8 percent gain in compensation in the second quarter was in line with forecasts of Wall Street economists surveyed by Reuters.
Wages and salaries, which account for about 70 percent of the overall index, also jumped 0.8 percent in the second quarter, after rising 0.9 percent in the first quarter.
Benefit costs rose 0.6 percent, compared with a 0.1 percent rise in the previous three-month period.
Despite the across-the-board gains, the overall pay and benefit increases showed no sign of accelerating from their recent pace.
Financial markets have been keeping close tabs on the index as they look for signs of whether employers have been forced to boost compensation packages to woo job seekers in a tight labour market.
Federal Reserve policy-makers, who raised short-term interest rates earlier this year to fend off inflationary threats, are keeping a close watch on labour costs.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan and other central bankers gave no hint in recent public appearances that they plan to raise interest rates any time soon.
On Friday, the Labour Department will release its monthly employment report, which will provide the government's first major look at economic activity in July.
In the 12 months ended June 30, total compensation rose 2.8 percent, compared with 2.9 percent in the 12 months ended June 30, 1996.
Wages and salaries in the 12 months ended June 30 rose 3.2 percent, after an identical gain in the 12-month period a year ago.
Employers' cost of providing benefits, including medical insurance, rose 2.0 percent in the 12 months ended June 30, after a 1.8 gain in the 12 months ended June 30, 1996.
